# Community guidelines

These community guidelines reflect the values and commitments of Open Source Europe. They aim to create a positive and productive community for all involved.

## Introduction

OSE is committed to keeping a respectful, inclusive, and supportive environment for all its members, participants, and stakeholders. These community guidelines set out how we expect people to behave and interact in our community.

***

## Scope

These community guidelines apply to all individuals participating in OSE activities, including members, partners, volunteers, and attendees at OSE events.

***

## Core Principles

* **Transparency**: Operate with transparency and integrity. Ensure that financial activities, decision-making processes, and communications are open and accessible.
* **Respect and Dignity**: Treat everyone with respect and dignity. Harassment, discrimination, or exclusionary behavior of any kind will not be tolerated.
* **Inclusivity**: Promote a welcoming environment where diversity is valued. Encourage participation from all individuals regardless of gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, disability, sexual orientation, or age.

***

## Expected Behavior

* **Collaboration**: Work together and support each other. Take part constructively and be open to different points of view.
* **Communication**: Communicate respectfully and professionally. Avoid offensive, inflammatory, or inappropriate language.
* **Responsibility**: Take responsibility for your actions and their impact on others. Address conflicts or issues promptly and respectfully.

***

## Unacceptable Behavior

* **Harassment**: Any form of harassment, including but not limited to sexual harassment, bullying, or intimidation.
* **Discrimination**: Discriminatory comments or actions based on personal characteristics or beliefs.
* **Disruption**: Intentional disruption of events, meetings, or online forums.

***

## Reporting and Enforcement

* **Reporting**: If you witness or experience behavior that violates these community guidelines, report it to the designated contact person immediately.
* **Investigation**: Reports will be taken seriously and investigated promptly and fairly.
* **Consequences**: Individuals who violate these community guidelines may face consequences, including warnings, expulsion from events, or removal from OSE activities.

***

## Safeguarding

OSE is committed to safeguarding the well-being of all participants. See our [Safeguarding Policy](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/safeguarding-policy/) for details of our safeguarding practices.

***

## Continuous Improvement

We keep improving our policies and practices. We welcome feedback and suggestions to improve this Code of Conduct. You can send them to our team.

***

## Contact Information

For questions, concerns, or to report a violation of this Code of Conduct, please contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

| A technical problem with Open Collective                       | Use [platform support](https://opencollective.com/help).                                                |

OSE aims to answer general questions within seven business days. This is a target, not a guaranteed response time. It does not replace the specific guidance for applications, payments or safeguarding.

## Expense follow-up and sensitive concerns

Use comments on the expense for routine questions about a submitted expense. Contact OSE privately for sensitive information.

For suspected misuse of funds or a problem involving Collective administrators, contact the OSE team directly in private at <home@opensourceeurope.org>. You do not need to go through the administrators concerned.

## Internal conflicts

Collectives manage their own internal conflicts. OSE intervenes when the situation affects funds or hosting conditions. It does not promise mediation.

# Mission, Vision & Impact areas

It all comes back to resilience

## Mission

Open Source Europe wants to make the social and solidarity economy and open source technologies sustainable. Our mission is to enable initiatives to raise and spend money transparently under a common umbrella nonprofit.

*Open Collective is an unusual company. In its ecosystem, a software company coexists with independent associations and foundations that we call 'hosts.' Open Source Europe is growing as one of the first major fiscal hosts on the European continent. We host initiatives that share our values and work towards a better future. Our values, and our vision for a healthy and thriving world, start with resilience. From that central concern come six related areas where we want to make a difference.*

### Resilient communities

Humanity is divided on countless fronts, but most will agree on the need for resilience. When systems fail, we need fallback buffers. Resilient communities don't break when one system failure causes the next. They have a patchwork of fallbacks to absorb the shocks. Resilience is when people next to you on the street know how to give CPR or can swim to save someone from drowning. It is when the families in your neighborhood own their own homes, and when your community has enough nurses to deliver your children and enough teachers to educate them. It is when every other house in your neighborhood has solar panels, feeding spare capacity back to the grid. When authorities arrive at a natural disaster, they find that the local community has already started helping itself. It is a society of ordinary people who are great leaders when they need to be. Resilience keeps people, jobs, and services in your hometown. And when we can trust our community to catch us if we fall, we can safely turn our attention to working for the greater good. That is why we put resilient communities at the center of our mission.

### Open innovation

When we use science and technology wisely, it makes us more resourceful. We expand our horizons and capabilities. If we share our findings, we grow stronger together. We encourage people to work together, and through the network effect we help knowledge and technology spread faster. Otherwise, we risk becoming divided by increasing technological gaps. Civil society is key to making innovation available to all. Distributed networks of passionate people around the world develop open-source software. Citizen scientists collect and share data. Civil engineers document how to build more energy-efficient homes. Technologists share blueprints for 3D printers and robots. Maker spaces around the world help people innovate and repair. Open innovation makes all of this possible.

### Commons stewardship

When a social innovation, cultural institution, or green space starts feeling like it has always been there, it has become a common good. We hope the commons we create will become so readily available that they appear unremarkable. And it is at exactly this point that it becomes vulnerable. Humankind longs for what is new and exciting. We want to solve the urgent problems of the day, and that is where we focus our attention. But we also need to pay attention to maintaining the solutions to problems we have already solved. Once saved from deforestation, a forest needs protection from invasive species. A community center built by one generation must be repaired and maintained by the next. Technology that encrypts websites and emails and keeps us safe from surveillance must be updated. We cannot take our commons for granted. If we do, all our work on communities, solidarity, culture, innovation, and ecologies risks being undone. For our progress to last, we need to support commons stewardship.

### Fiscal hosting in Europe and beyond

We are based in Europe but offer fiscal hosting to initiatives around the world. If our vision speaks to you, get in touch. We are ready to host your collective today and would be excited to hear from you. [You can apply here.](https://opencollective.com/europe/apply)

# Risk and Compliance aspects

Open Source Europe: Grant Eligibility and Risk Assessment Policy

## Introduction

Open Source Europe (OSE) is committed to supporting initiatives that promote positive social change and a more just world. This policy sets out the criteria we use to assess whether grant proposals are eligible. It also sets out how we find possible compliance risks linked to terrorism/extremism financing.

***

## Grant Eligibility Criteria

OSE prioritizes proposals from initiatives that:

* Operate in accordance with the law.
* Do not support or glorify terrorist groups.
* Show that they manage money responsibly, including transparent record-keeping and reporting.

***

## Compliance Risk Assessment

OSE assesses potential compliance risks associated with grant proposals using the following factors (in order of importance):

1. **Beneficiary Impact**: Can the initiative show that its work benefits its target communities?
2. **Public Statements**: Does the initiative's public messaging avoid promoting violence or extremism?
3. **Transparency**: Does the initiative publish financial statements and reports on its activities?
4. **Legality**: Do the initiative's mission and activities comply with legal frameworks and international law?

***

## Contextual Considerations

OSE takes context into account when it evaluates proposals. It carries out due diligence to understand the specific circumstances and actions of the initiative.

***

## Information Sources

To assess grant proposals, OSE uses different information sources, including (in order of importance):&#x20;

* Initiative websites and reports.
* Credible news sources and independent research organizations.
* United Nations and human rights organization reports.
* Government watchlists and sanctions lists.

***

## Limited Veto Power

OSE reserves the right to propose a veto of a grant proposal if a high compliance risk is identified based on the criteria above. A clear and documented reason will be provided, which sets out the specific concerns.

***

## Appeals Process

Initiatives have the right to appeal a veto decision. The appeals process will be clearly explained to all applicants.

***

## Policy Review and Revision

This policy is reviewed and revised periodically, to make sure it stays effective and in line with best practices.

***

## Conclusion

OSE is committed to balancing the prevention of terrorism financing with support for legitimate initiatives that work towards positive social change. This policy is the framework for that goal.

***

## Need Assistance?

For questions or more information about risk and compliance aspects, please contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Safeguarding Policy

## Introduction

Open Source Europe (OSE) is committed to creating a safe and inclusive environment for all staff, volunteers, partners, and beneficiaries. This policy outlines our commitment to safeguarding and sets out procedures for reporting and responding to concerns.

***

## What is Safeguarding?

Safeguarding refers to the actions we take to protect people, especially children and vulnerable adults, from harm. This includes protection from:

* Abuse (physical, sexual, emotional, neglect)
* Exploitation
* Neglect
* Discrimination
* Bullying

***

## Our Commitment

OSE is committed to:

* Promoting a culture of safety and well-being for everyone involved in our activities.
* Sharing safeguarding guidance with staff and volunteers, including how to report concerns and their role in protecting people.
* Providing clear procedures for reporting concerns.
* Taking all concerns seriously and having the safeguarding leads review them to determine appropriate next steps.
* Supporting anyone who has been affected by safeguarding incidents.

***

## Who is Vulnerable?

Safeguarding applies to everyone, but some people may be more vulnerable to harm. This includes:

* Children
* People with disabilities
* Older adults
* People who are dependent on others

***

## Reporting Concerns

Anyone who has a concern about the safety or well-being of someone involved in OSE activities should report it immediately. This applies even if they are not sure about the nature of the concern.

Contact the safeguarding leads listed below to report a concern. OSE does not provide a continuously staffed reporting service or guarantee a response time.

***

## How to Report a Concern

Concerns can be reported to:

* Safeguarding leads:
  * Ivan Cukeric: <ivan@opencollective.com>
  * Jean-François De Hertogh: <jf@opencollective.com>

If a concern involves one of the safeguarding leads, contact the other lead directly, provided they are not also involved.

Reports can be made in person, by email, or in writing. Information is shared only with those who need it to handle the concern or where disclosure is required by law. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised.

***

## What Happens When a Concern is Reported?

All reported concerns are taken seriously. The safeguarding leads review each report and determine appropriate next steps, including referral to external services or relevant authorities where necessary. OSE does not systematically conduct an internal investigation.

Depending on the circumstances, appropriate action may include:

* Referral to relevant authorities
* Disciplinary action
* Support for the person who raised the concern or the person at risk

***

## Confidentiality

OSE limits the sharing of information about safeguarding concerns to those who need it to handle the concern or where disclosure is required by law. Absolute confidentiality cannot be promised.

***

## Support

OSE listens to people affected by safeguarding incidents and directs them towards appropriate support services. OSE does not organise or fund psychological counselling.

***

## Training

OSE shares safeguarding guidance with staff and volunteers, including how to respond to and report concerns. OSE does not currently provide systematic safeguarding training.

***

## Review

This policy will be reviewed regularly to ensure it remains effective.

***

## Need Assistance?

For any questions about this policy or safeguarding in general, please contact the safeguarding lead at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

# Terminology

We use some terms to describe processes in the Open Collective ecosystem. Please use these terms instead of 'user' when you create issues or support requests. Everyone is a user!

## Individuals

Everyone interacting with the Open Collective platform is considered an individual. Individuals can take on different roles in the ecosystem:

* **Contributor**: Someone who supports an initiative, with money or in other ways.
* **Organizer**: An individual who creates or manages an initiative.

## Financial Contributors

### Organizational Financial Contributor

A company or organization that supports an initiative financially, often at a higher tier. These contributors are often called sponsors. They may want benefits such as brand exposure, community goodwill, or tangible perks.

### Individual Financial Contributor

An individual who supports an initiative financially, with one-time or recurring contributions. They may find initiatives through:

* Open Collective's homepage
* Direct links to a Collective
* Organizer's page

### Expense Submitter

An individual who requests payment from an initiative's budget using the expense function. This can be to get paid back for purchases made for the initiative, or to get paid for completed work.

## Non-Financial Contributors

### Organizer

An individual who creates or works on an initiative. After they talk with our team, organizers decide whether they are creating a 'Fund' or a 'Collective'.

### Core Contributor

Individuals who are major contributors and represent the Collective on its page as part of the team.

### Collective Admin

A type of Core Contributor with additional permissions, allowing them to:

* Edit the Collective
* Change settings
* Approve expenses
* Make financial contributions to other Collectives
* Receive messages from people trying to contact the Collective

Core Contributors aim to make their communities financially sustainable, using tools like tiers, goals, and social media sharing. They focus on managing and growing their communities by creating events and sending updates.

### Event Attendee

Individuals who register to attend a Collective's event, often arriving through direct links provided by event organizers.

## Initiatives

Initiatives are accounts for projects or groups hosted by Open Source Europe. An initiative can be either a Collective or a Fund. During the application process, our team will help you choose the right account type for your project.

### Collective

A Collective represents a project or group with a mission or purpose, raising and spending funds transparently to achieve their goals.

## Fiscal Hosts

A Fiscal Host, or Sponsor, is a type of Organization that lets Collectives handle money without having to legally incorporate. The Fiscal Host holds a Collective’s funds in their bank account and can generate invoices and receipts for Financial Contributors. Think of a Fiscal Host as an umbrella organization for the Collectives it supports.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# About Open Source Europe

Open Source Europe is a Belgian association. It is the fiscal host for over 400 initiatives and works with philanthropic institutions to support regranting around the world.

***

## Service Overview

Unlike traditional non-profits, Open Source Europe (OSE) combines a legal structure with its own digital infrastructure. Together they make the following possible:

* Fiscal hosting for open source projects. We give developers, maintainers and communities a legal umbrella, so they can operate without creating their own legal entity.
* Grant distribution and fund management. We manage funds for foundations and companies that want to support critical open source projects in Europe and beyond.
* Radical transparency. All financial activity is public on the Open Collective platform, which builds trust and accountability in the community.

***

## How hosting works

OSE provides a Belgian nonprofit home for open source projects. We use the Open Collective platform to manage budgets, receive contributions and process expenses transparently.

See our [Terms of Service](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) for the hosting agreement.

***

## Who We Serve

* Project maintainers of open source projects that have no legal structure of their own.
* Funders and corporates, such as international companies that want a trusted intermediary to support open source in Europe.
* Developer networks, meaning communities that want fiscal and operational support for their collective activities.

***

## How to Work With Us

* Projects can apply for fiscal hosting to start receiving donations and grants legally.
* Funders can support projects and manage their contributions transparently through our hosted funds.
* Organizations can manage large-scale distributions efficiently, without complex international structures.

***

[Contact the team](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org)

***

## A little history

Open Source Europe grew out of Open Collective Europe's fiscal hosting work. As that work grew, OSE became the home for open source projects and communities. Open Collective Europe Foundation developed its wider philanthropic activities. Our hosting agreement still uses the association's name, Open Collective Europe ASBL/vzw.

Today, OSE focuses on helping open source communities receive funding, pay contributors and manage their projects transparently.

# Contributions FAQ

Questions about contributing to our hosted collectives

## **How do I cancel recurring donations/subscriptions/payments?**

See our instructions on how to cancel recurring or ongoing donations, subscriptions, payments, etc., [here](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#change-the-amount-payment-method-or-cancel-an-existing-contribution).

## **What if a contributor wants their contribution to be anonymous?**

Contributors can make an anonymous payment by choosing [incognito](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#profile) when they pick a profile to pay from. If the contributor pays as a [guest](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/payments#contributing-as-a-guest), the given name still shows up. The contributor just does not have to log in to make the payment. All Open Collective users can also [separate](https://opencollective.com/opencollective/updates/new-legal-and-display-name-settings) a public display name from their private legal name.

## **What if a financial contributor is unable or not comfortable with submitting their credit card information online?**

If a donor is not comfortable with online credit card transactions, they can send the funds via PayPal or bank transfer.

## **Someone said they sent my collective money but I don’t see it in my account! Help?**

\~or\~

## **I sent in money but I don't see my donation on the collective's page?!**

[Contact us!](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/contact-us/)

We often receive money in our bank account without any sign of where it should go. This is why it is so important to include the order number in the bank transfer. We always search carefully for the right collective, but sometimes we cannot find it.

At the end of the month, we move the unidentified funds to a [holding fund](https://opencollective.com/oce-holding-fund).

We keep the money there until we can identify who it is intended for and then we transfer it.

Write to us on <home@opensourceeurope.org> or send us a message on [Discord](https://discord.gg/TmbRzFBqBa). We will ask you for screenshots or receipts that show the expected amount, the collective name, and the sender or any other information about the bank transfer. With these, we can send the funds to the right collective.

## **What if a financial contributor requests an invoice before making the donation?**

OSE can confirm receipt of a donation, but a donation confirmation is not a sales or VAT invoice. OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before you commit to sales, invoiced services or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE. Discuss with OSE whether it can support the arrangement and under what conditions. Do this before you make commitments or receive payment. Acceptance is not guaranteed.

## **Can we use outside fundraising platforms to fundraise for our collective?**

Open Collective already includes crowdfunding tools and is the usual option. External platforms such as Patreon, Ko-fi or GoFundMe are considered case by case. Contact OSE before you set up a campaign to receive funds through OSE. The team checks payout arrangements, supporting records and any promised benefits. Compatibility and acceptance are not automatic.

See [GitHub Sponsors](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/setting-up-github-sponsors/) for that specific route.

## Can we receive earned income (i.e., non-donations)?

OSE primarily supports donations and grants. Before you commit to sales, invoiced services or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE. Discuss with OSE whether it can support the arrangement and under what conditions. Do this before you make commitments or receive payment. Acceptance is not guaranteed.

## **Can we offer financial contributors something in return for their donation?**

Tiers can suggest contribution amounts. If you intend to promise goods, services, advertising, access or another benefit, contact OSE before you commit or receive funds. The team will check whether it can support the arrangement. Acceptance is not guaranteed. You can still acknowledge donors, as long as the acknowledgment is optional and not promised as part of a tier.

## **Can my group offer memberships/accept membership fees?**

A symbolic supporter membership gives no rights or benefits. Any proposed membership with benefits must be discussed with OSE before you commit to it or collect fees. Acceptance is not automatic.

## Can my collective donate to another hosted collective?

Transfers to another hosted Collective are different from ordinary external donations. Before you go ahead, get OSE’s approval of the recipient, purpose and funding conditions. Collectives[ can give to other collectives](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/collective-to-collective) hosted by Open Source Europe. (If you want to give to a collective with another fiscal host, there are[ some extra steps](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/financial-contributors/collective-to-collective#across-different-fiscal-hosts).)

## U.S. tax-deductible donations

The established Myriad → OCEF → OSE route supports U.S. tax-deductible giving, subject to applicable tax rules. Contact OSE before payment to organise the right route. See [U.S. giving](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/what-we-offer/tax-deductible-giving-for-us-donors/).

## Donation refunds

Contact the Collective administrators first. They forward the request to OSE. If they do not respond, contact OSE directly. Contact does not guarantee a refund. See [Refunds](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/refunds/).

# Fiscal Hosting FAQs

## What is a Fiscal Host?

A **Fiscal Host** is an organization that holds funds on behalf of Collectives, so they can operate financially without having to set up a legal entity.

This arrangement is also called fiscal sponsorship. It allows your Collective to:

* Receive and manage donations and grants
* Provide donation confirmations and administer grants
* Handle taxes, bookkeeping, and legal compliance
* Pay expenses approved by your Collective admins

The Open Collective platform provides all the tools to manage these flows transparently.

***

## How do I add a Fiscal Host to my Collective?

If your Collective does not yet have a Fiscal Host, you can add one by:

1. Going to your Collective page
2. Clicking on **“Apply to Fiscal Host”**
3. Choosing the appropriate Host (such as Open Source Europe)

> **Note:** Learn how: [Add a Fiscal Host](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/add-fiscal-host)

***

## More Info

See [How to apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) and our [Terms of Service](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) for hosting with OSE.

## Moving to another fiscal host

Contact OSE before you leave. You then coordinate with the new host, settle outstanding expenses and check the conditions for transferring the balance. Transfers remain subject to the hosting agreement and restrictions on the funds. A change on Open Collective does not automatically change your GitHub Sponsors setup.

## Closing a Collective voluntarily

If the Collective stops operating without moving to another host, settle outstanding expenses first. The Collective then proposes where the remaining balance goes, in line with its purpose. OSE reviews and approves it according to the funding conditions.

## Inactive Collectives

When a Collective is inactive for a long time, OSE contacts the administrators and sends reminders. The reminders state a deadline to respond and what happens if there is no reply. If there is no response, OSE may end hosting, stop recurring contributions and reallocate the balance to its general fund or a similar project. This happens under the applicable agreement and funding restrictions. There is no universal six-month timeline. This process is separate from unidentified incoming payments.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# General FAQs

## What can I do with an Open Source Europe account?

By joining Open Source Europe, your initiative can:

* Collect recurring or one-off donations
* Apply for subsidies or grants
* Pay invoices and reimburse expenses
* Offer full budget transparency to your community
* Operate without creating your own legal entity
* Pay service providers on compliant invoices, including through workers’ cooperatives; reimburse eligible volunteer expenses

***

## What am I not allowed to do?

To stay compliant with our legal and charitable framework, you may not:

* Issue invoices or sign documents in the name of OSE. Any specific contract that needs OSE’s signature must be discussed and accepted beforehand. Do not use OSE’s legal name or VAT number to have supplier invoices issued for your Collective
* Use funds to influence legislation or politics (lobbying)
* Support or engage in illegal activity
* Use funds for personal profit
* Have another fiscal host at the same time. Technical or community affiliations may be accepted after review
* Spend funds on purposes outside your initiative’s mission. If you do, they must be reimbursed

***

## Why should I use Open Collective?

Open Source Europe uses the Open Collective platform to make financial management simpler and more transparent.

Benefits include:

* Easy collection of recurring or one-off contributions
* Simple spending: submit a receipt/invoice → approve → paid
* Automatic and public budget tracking
* Shared financial visibility, which builds collaboration and trust

> We believe transparency makes communities more resilient and democratic.

***

## How is Open Source Europe different?

OSE differs in these ways:

* Designed for collaborative communities, as well as for campaigns or individuals
* Open source, with built-in transparency (no hidden ledgers)
* We provide fiscal hosting as a service using a nonprofit legal framework
* Based in Europe, but globally connected

***

## How much does it cost?

The current OSE hosting fees are:

| Contribution type                                                 | OSE fee |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| Ordinary online crowdfunding donations by card (Stripe) or PayPal | 8%      |
| Incoming bank transfers                                           | 10%     |
| Grants and public subsidies                                       | 10%     |
| Tax-deductible donations through the supported intermediary route | 10%     |
| GitHub Sponsors                                                   | 10%     |

For ordinary card and PayPal donations, the 8% OSE hosting fee is calculated on the donation amount before payment processing fees are deducted. For example, a €20 donation has a €1.60 OSE hosting fee. Payment processing fees are separate and also reduce the amount available to the Collective. Their amount may vary.

Currency conversion services or intermediaries may have additional costs. Contact OSE to confirm the costs applicable to a specific route. This page does not say how the fee is calculated for other routes, and it gives no combined fee rate.

These are the current rates. This page does not introduce any fee reduction.

***

## Can we get a discount?

We’re often asked for fee reductions, and we understand why.\
Many initiatives bring in funds already raised, and we know how tight nonprofit budgets can be.

However, our standard fees are already kept as low as possible to cover the real costs of:

* Legal & administrative management
* Risk and compliance
* Payments, reports, and support over time

> **Caution:** Outside of specific exceptional cases (like COVID-19 or Ukrainian relief), we cannot offer fee waivers or discounts.

***

## What if I want to become my own fiscal host someday?

No problem! You're welcome to use Open Source Europe as your fiscal host for as long as you need and remain eligible.

* You can ask to end fiscal hosting, following the notice and remaining-balance rules in your [hosting agreement](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/).
* If you plan to move to managing your own structure, we can help you prepare.
* The [Open Collective platform](https://opencollective.com/) also supports organizations that wish to become fiscal hosts themselves.

***

## How long does it take to get started?

* The application process only takes a few minutes.
* We might reach out with a few follow-up questions.
* Once your application is accepted, you can start receiving donations right away.

> **Note:** Completing the application and being accepted are separate steps. See [How to apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) for the review process and indicative response time. Additional information may be required before acceptance.

***

## Is there a minimum required budget?

Nope! There is no minimum balance required to be hosted by OSE.

Since our fees are taken as a percentage of incoming contributions, you can start small and grow as your initiative develops.

## Paying collaborators

Collectives can pay service providers against a compliant invoice, including through a workers’ cooperative. Agree the work, price and dates with the Collective and submit the invoice through Open Collective for review. OSE does not provide a standard employment or payroll service. Any arrangement requiring OSE to sign a specific contract must be discussed and accepted beforehand.

## Discounts and nonprofit benefits

OSE may support a request or provide an attestation on a case-by-case basis. Hosting does not automatically qualify a Collective for every nonprofit discount or benefit. Each supplier sets its own eligibility criteria; OSE cannot guarantee acceptance.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Application Questions

## Prepare Your Answers Before Applying

Prepare your answers to the following questions before you apply to Open Source Europe (OSE). This makes the application faster and easier, and helps you explain the purpose of your initiative.

***

## Required Information

* **Location:** Give the city and country where your initiative is mainly based. OSE hosts initiatives all over the world, but knowing your location helps us support you better.
* **Your Name and Email Address:** Give your full name and a valid email address where we can contact you.
* **Collective Name:** Choose a unique name for your collective that describes it.
* **Website and/or Social Media Links:** Share links that show your initiative’s activities and online presence.
* **Unique URL:** You can choose a unique URL for your collective’s page on the Open Collective platform.
* **Administrators:** One administrator is enough, and two are recommended for shared management and continuity. Use real names. Administrators have full permissions to manage the collective’s settings and finances.

***

## Application Questions

Prepare short answers (about 250 characters) to the following questions:

1. **Duration:** How long has your collective been operating?
2. **Fundraising to Date:** If you’ve started fundraising, how much have you raised so far?
3. **Fundraising Goals:** What is your target fundraising amount?
4. **Funding Sources:** Who do you anticipate will fund your initiative?
5. **Collective Activities:** Briefly describe what your collective does.
6. **Mission Alignment:** Explain how your collective furthers one or more of OSE’s mission impact areas.

***

## Tips for a Successful Application

* Keep your answers clear and to the point.
* Show how your initiative contributes to the public good and fits OSE’s mission.
* Include links to your work, such as project websites, social media pages or articles, to support your application.
* Check your answers for clarity and completeness before you submit your application.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have questions or need help with the application process, [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Eligibility

## Who Can Apply to Be Hosted by Open Source Europe?

Open Source Europe (OSE) welcomes initiatives from around the world that align with our mission and values. OSE supports open source projects and communities. Your application should explain how your activities contribute to open source.

***

## Eligibility Criteria

To be eligible for fiscal hosting by OSE, your initiative must:

* Align with OSE's mission and impact areas. Your activities should be charitable and aim to benefit the public.
* Be non-profit. Profits must not be distributed to members. For the types of contributions accepted through OSE, including the rules on membership benefits and other counterparty benefits, see [Contributions FAQ](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/faq/contributions-faq/).
* Have no separate legal entity. Initiatives with their own legal status, such as registered NGOs, are not eligible. Such entities can still launch a Fund with OSE for specific programs.
* Have at least one administrator. One is enough, and two are recommended for shared management and continuity. Administrators use real names.
* Keep to appropriate content standards. Content that promotes violence, hate speech, pornography, or any other material considered inappropriate or offensive is not permitted.

***

## Global Reach

OSE is based in Europe, but it supports initiatives all over the world. Where your project is based does not affect your eligibility, as long as you meet the criteria above.

***

## Not Required

OSE aims to lower barriers for initiatives with impact, so we do not require:

* Application fees
* A minimum budget balance
* A minimum annual fundraising amount
* A fixed duration of commitment
* Complex reporting requirements (an annual update on your collective page is enough)

***

## Important Considerations

* OSE administers funds on behalf of your initiative under the hosting agreement. If you move to another host or close, contact OSE to agree how outstanding expenses and the remaining balance are handled under the applicable agreement and funding restrictions.
* OSE assesses possible compliance risks of initiatives. It checks that initiatives align with legal frameworks and avoid activities that could be linked to terrorism or extremism financing.

***

## Ready to Apply?

If your initiative meets the criteria above, follow our [How to Apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/) guide to start your application.

If you have questions, [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Affiliation with another organisation

OSE does not accept fiscal hosting at the same time as another host. OSE may accept a technical or community affiliation with another organisation after review. Affiliation alone does not mean fiscal hosting.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# How to apply

Use this guide to prepare and submit a hosting application, and to learn how OSE reviews it.

## Start here

1. Read the [eligibility criteria](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/eligibility/), [hosting fees](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/faq/general-faqs/#how-much-does-it-cost) and [application questions](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/application-questions/).
2. Prepare your project details and at least one administrator. We recommend two.
3. Follow the application process below, then complete the supplementary form that OSE provides.

Next, OSE aims to give a first response within seven business days after it receives the completed supplementary form. This is a target for the response, not a deadline for acceptance. After acceptance, continue with [your first steps](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/basics/).

## Join Open Source Europe in just a few steps

Applying to be hosted by Open Source Europe (OSE) is simple and usually takes a few minutes. After OSE accepts you, you can receive contributions and manage your initiative in the open on the Open Collective platform.

***

## Before You Apply

Check that your initiative meets these criteria:

* It aligns with OSE's mission and impact areas. Your activities should be charitable and aim to benefit the public.
* It has at least one administrator. One is enough, and two are recommended for shared management and continuity. Use real names.
* It has no legal entity of its own, separate from OSE.
* It can be based anywhere in the world, not only in Europe.

Also read our [Terms of Cooperation](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) and [Community Guidelines](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/about/community-guidelines/).

***

## Application Process

1. Go to the [Open Source Europe profile](https://opencollective.com/europe) and click "Apply".
2. Choose your collective type:
   * If you are new to the Open Collective platform, select "Create New Collective".
   * If you already have a collective, choose it from the list.
3. Complete the application form. Give information about your initiative, including:
   * Location
   * Name and email address
   * Collective name
   * Website and/or social media links
   * Brief description of your collective's activities
   * Explanation of how your collective furthers OSE's mission impact areas
4. Add at least one administrator. Two are recommended for shared management and continuity.
5. Review your information, accept the terms of service and submit your application.

You can edit all this information later, so it does not need to be perfect.

***

## After Submission

To complete the review, the team gives you a supplementary application form. Do not wait for an automatic email.

We aim to give a first response within seven business days of receiving your completed supplementary form. The review may take longer if we need more information. This does not guarantee acceptance, or that the review ends within seven days.

After acceptance, you can start to receive contributions. We offer an optional welcome call after acceptance. You can receive contributions without it. The welcome email includes documentation and an invitation to book a call. After a call, the team sends a recap and useful links.

***

## Transitioning from Another Fiscal Host

If you are moving from another fiscal host:

* If you use the Open Collective platform, the move is fairly simple.
* If you do not use the Open Collective platform, the process depends on what your current organization requires. Usually, they can transfer your funds to OSE, and you can start quickly.

Tell both OSE and your current fiscal host about your plans before you apply, so that the move goes smoothly.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have questions or need help with the application process, [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Ask OSE from your AI tools

The OSE knowledge base searches these docs and answers questions about OSE with cited sources. You can ask it in the chat at Ask OSE (link removed: /ask/), or connect it to your own AI assistant. The knowledge base then runs on your own computer, so OSE does not see your questions.

All three ways start the knowledge base with `uvx`, so install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) first.

## Use it as an MCP server

Add the server to any MCP client, such as Claude Code, Cursor or Claude Desktop. In Claude Code, run this command:

```bash
claude mcp add ose-knowledge -- uvx ose-knowledge-mcp==0.12.13
```

For another client, put this in the client's configuration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ose-knowledge": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["ose-knowledge-mcp==0.12.13"]
    }
  }
}
```

The version is fixed, so you always get a known build. Each OSE release updates the version on this page.

## Use it as a Claude Code plugin

The plugin adds the MCP server, an `ose-researcher` agent and an `ask-about-ose` skill. The skill sends your OSE questions to the agent. You can also call the skill as `/ose-knowledge:ask-about-ose`.

```text
/plugin marketplace add opensourceeurope/ose-ai
/plugin install ose-knowledge@ose-ai
```

## Use it as a Codex plugin

The same plugin installs in Codex with the MCP server and the `ask-about-ose` skill. Codex does not load the `ose-researcher` agent, so the skill searches the knowledge base itself.

```bash
codex plugin marketplace add opensourceeurope/ose-ai
```

Then run `/plugins` in Codex, install `ose-knowledge` and start a new session. To install from the terminal instead, run `codex plugin add ose-knowledge@ose-ai` and start a new session.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Deciding on How to Use Your Money

How to use funds for your initiative on OSE

This guide is based on an Open Source Collective workshop led by Sumana Harihareswara of Changeset Consulting in January 2022. It helped open source software projects hosted on Open Collective decide how to use the money they had already raised. We adapted it to the cases we see on OSE, and all examples are in EUR.

## Why You Should (or Shouldn't) Spend Your Money

### Reasons to Spend

* Advance your project. Pay for tasks, chores and infrastructure improvements that are hard to do with volunteer labour alone.
* Attract more donors. When you spend money, donors see that you use their contributions well.
* Experiment and learn. Spending money on pilot projects or services can help you try new approaches and gives you more flexibility.
* Boost morale. Small purchases of merchandise (stickers, awards, t-shirts) can help contributors stay and can improve team morale.

In general, you can spend less than 10% of your saved funds without a long decision process. The same goes for a one-time expense of less than 20% of your stable recurring monthly income.

### **Reasons to Save:**

* Specific activities. Save up for large expenses, such as hiring contractors.
* Self-insurance. Keep funds to cover possible risks, such as unexpected hosting costs or legal expenses.
* Budgeting. Make a budget that sets funds aside for self-insurance and for future activities. Then you know clearly how much you can spend.

## Driver and Supporter/Protector Activities

**Drivers:** Activities that directly advance your mission (e.g., software development).

**Supporters:** Infrastructure activities and purchases that support drivers (e.g., organising conferences, buying laptops).

**Protectors:** Activities or expenses that reduce risks (e.g., legal fees, code of conduct workshops).

For instance, in this diagram...

[Image removed: Diagram of money and resources flowing into a project from creators, individual users, platforms and organisational users, and out to platforms and services, labour, convenings and travel, equipment and supplies, and outgoing donations and grants]

*Money and Resources, shown by those that go into a project and then what comes out of it*

...labor for software development is a driver, because writing the software directly advances the mission of making and improving the open source project. An example of a supporter activity: organizing a conference where the contributors can meet to improve and speed up their work. An example of a supporter purchase: buying a new laptop for a contributor to use.

## Advancing Your Goals and Roadmap

Consider what's on your roadmap and how you can spend to support it.

If your project has no clear goals or written roadmap, you can still spend money on the following:

* Consultants who help you create a roadmap.
* Hardware upgrades for your team's development environment.
* Mentorship programs, where you sponsor and mentor interns to build capacity.
* Volunteer contributions. Organise volunteers around your activity and reimburse them according to the law in their country of residence.

If you have a roadmap, pay new contractors or services to take repetitive tasks off your existing volunteers.

### Specific Spending Examples

* Independent contractors
* Volunteer reimbursements
* Professional education and tools
* Meet up travel expenses
* Logo design and merchandise
* Co-working space
* Virtual assistant services

### Hiring Contractors

You can hire collaborators for your collective as contractors. You can choose who to hire informally or through a public job posting. See [the invoicing options](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/invoices-or-reimbursements/).

### Using Bounties Cautiously

Patch bounty programs can encourage specific development work. They may also make people compete instead of working together. Use bounties for tasks that volunteers do not want to do or do not have the skills for.

## Decision-Making and Governance

Open Collective's expense documentation says:

> **Note:** "The decision is up to you as a project. Some projects are informal, and any Core Contributor can approve any expense. Others have a formal decision-making or budgeting process, or only pay expenses for specific things. We advise you to have a discussion with your collaborators and agree on guidelines for approving expenses."

Also read the documentation on [budget](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/budget) and [expense policies](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/collective-settings/expense-policy), and ["ten ways to make decisions about money"](https://blog.opencollective.com/ten-ways-to-make-decisions-about-money/).

* Common concerns:

  * Legal or tax questions: Open Source Europe cannot advise you on the legal or tax obligations of your members or collaborators. We recommend that you contact a legal or tax specialist in their country of residence. For general guidance, use this documentation or contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.
  * Disagreements: act in good faith and support decisions made by the group. Clear policies and consistent practices help a lot.

  People will have reasonable concerns about what you spent, and why and how you spent it. If you are not sure how to prevent or answer those concerns, you have two main options:

  * *Intense up-front transparency*: publish the details of your decisions openly. Tell contributors and observers about possible expenses in advance, make clear who decides, and offer a public comment period before approval. Do this every time, and use Open Collective's tools to keep the records available for later review. This is fairly easy if you manage all expenses through Open Collective invoices.
  * *Post-decision accountability*: do not offer a public comment period before the decision. Instead, run a clear private comment period among the people who decide. Then answer for past expenses: anyone who wants to can ask for details about a specific expense. This lets you make more decisions privately, and you can give some details privately when people ask. Keep in mind that your payees, or the people you answer, may publish details on their own.

## OSE’s role in conflicts

Collectives manage their internal conflicts. OSE intervenes if a situation affects funds or hosting conditions, but does not promise mediation. If you suspect misuse of funds, or have concerns about administrators, contact OSE privately. You do not have to go through those administrators.


<!-- opencrane:page -->

# Basics

This is your starting point after OSE accepts your Collective. Work through the essentials, then use the relevant guide for each transaction.

## Your first steps

1. Check your public profile and contacts. Use the platform's [Quick Start Guide](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/quick-start-guide). Keep administrator access and the main contact up to date, and notify OSE of changes.
2. Choose how to receive funds. Start with [donations and funding routes](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/financial-contributions-how-to-donate/). You can receive contributions without waiting for the optional welcome call.
3. Agree how your Collective makes spending decisions. Read [budget decisions](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/guides/deciding-on-how-to-use-your-money/).
4. Prepare your first payment. Use [Pay and get reimbursed](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/). Funds must be received and available before payment.
5. Keep the community informed. Use Updates and review the responsibilities below.

Some steps need OSE's agreement first. Contact the team before a grant application naming OSE as recipient or signatory, a specific contract OSE would sign, or a proposed commercial arrangement. Details follow below.

## Welcome to Open Source Europe!

Once your application to be hosted by Open Source Europe (OSE) is approved, you can immediately start managing your Collective on the Open Collective platform. Welcome aboard!

***

## Top 5 Things to Remember

1. Contracts and agreements: Before any arrangement requires OSE to sign a specific contract, discuss it with OSE and get its acceptance.
2. Grant applications: If OSE will be named as recipient or signatory, contact the team before submission so it can review and accept its role and commitments.
3. Community updates: Use the Updates feature to keep your community informed. Publish at least one update per year.
4. Expenses: Follow the [expense guide](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/how-it-works/expenses/) for documents, review and payment.
5. Contributions: OSE mainly supports donations and grants. Before committing to sales, invoiced services or contributions with promised benefits, contact OSE to discuss whether the arrangement can be supported and under what conditions. Do this before making commitments or receiving payment. Acceptance is not guaranteed.

***

## Understanding Open Collective

Open Collective is the platform that OSE operates on. It provides tools for transparent budgeting, customizing a Collective profile, setting up tiers and goals, and more.

For an overview of using the Open Collective platform, check out its [documentation](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/about/documentation). It explains the features you can use.

Its [Quick Start Guide](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/quick-start-guide) is another good place to start.

***

## Budget Management of Your Collective

Receiving funds and submitting expenses are both simple. Each has its own page in these docs with the details. Feel free to share them with the contributors and members of your Collective.

Being fiscally hosted by OSE means joining a community of hundreds of initiatives that share the same tools to manage their independent projects. It needs little attention, but it does need some to work properly.

Please read the guidelines on [donations](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/collectives/raising-money) and [expenses](https://docs.opencollective.com/help/expenses-and-getting-paid/submitting-expenses). If you have any questions or doubts, contact us at <home@opensourceeurope.org>.

***

## Important Notes

* Tax obligations: You’re responsible for understanding and fulfilling all of your tax obligations. If you’re not sure whether you need to charge or pay tax, we encourage you to ask a tax professional about your tax obligations. OSE can’t provide tax advice.
* Terms & Conditions: Please review our [Terms & Conditions](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/terms-of-service/) for detailed information about your responsibilities and our policies.

***

## Need Assistance?

If you have any questions or need help, feel free to [contact us](mailto:home@opensourceeurope.org).

## Keeping your contacts up to date

When administrators or the main contact change, update access on Open Collective and notify OSE so the team can keep supporting you without a break.

## Optional welcome call

After acceptance, OSE offers an optional welcome call. Contributions can start without waiting for the call. See [How to apply](https://opensourceeurope.org/docs/getting-started/how-to-apply/).
